completion_data.completion_summary: Built hooks/validate-no-record-versioning.sh (a PreToolUse Write|Edit hook blocking BLOCKING-tier record-versioning language via exit 2, advisory-silent, payload-only, fail-open), its fixture test, restored the lint/hook scope-agreement case in test-check-record-versioning.sh, registered it bare on both settings surfaces plus manifest.json, truth-ed up the taxonomy's Enforcement section, and redeployed with four live probes all confirming correct behavior.

memory_candidates.content: check-record-versioning.sh's (and check-task-references.sh's) PATH_SCOPE mode enumerates files via `git ls-files PATH_SCOPE` -- scoping a self-check to a single brand-new, not-yet-git-tracked file silently returns zero rows and reports a false-clean 0 BLOCKING/0 ADVISORY, not a [SKIP] or an error. When self-checking a newly created deliverable against one of this repo's write-time lints before its first commit, either run the lint unscoped (full-repo) or `git add` the file first -- a PATH_SCOPE-scoped pre-commit self-check on an untracked file proves nothing.

A hook/lint whose header prose documents the forbidden language it detects is itself a deliverable subject to that same rule, and risks tripping on its own documentation once live. Concretely, hooks/validate-no-record-versioning.sh's header originally quoted the literal phrase 'supersedes v1' as a forbidden-category example, which matched its own RV_SUPERSESSION_ERE pattern and would have made the file unblockable-to-edit after deployment -- caught only by a full-repo lint scan after the file was git-tracked, not by an earlier PATH_SCOPE-scoped self-check (see the companion PATH_SCOPE memory). When documenting a detector's own forbidden patterns in its header/docstring, either paraphrase around the literal trigger shape or wrap the example in the detector's own marker-exemption convention.
